extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, judges, and advanced students of patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and doctrines governing when and how a United States patent may be amended or re-issued to correct omissions, misstatements, or to broaden claims. Covers requirements about inadvertence, delay (laches), intervening rights, identity of subject-matter, and limits on adding new matter or new uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue authorized to correct inadvertence, accident, or mistake
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue for the purpose of enlarging claims which were unduly restricted in the original is authorized by statute whenever the original restriction arose from inadvertence, accident, or mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor who actually invented more than his original patent secured may obtain a re-issue to correct inadvertent omissions or misstatements. But the re-issue must be sought in a period consistent with an original intention to protect the invention (i.e., without unreasonable delay). See discussion and cases collected (e.g., many post-1880 decisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot embrace new matter not disclosed in the original specification
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot embrace new matter under any circumstances; matter not described in the original specification cannot be inserted in the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts repeatedly hold that new matter may never be claimed in a re-issue. The re-issue is limited to correcting errors in the original disclosure/claims and cannot add subject-matter that was not originally described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of matter clearly described but not claimed indicates intentional abandonment unless promptly remedied
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission from the claims of matter that was clearly described in the original patent indicates, prima facie, an intention to abandon that matter unless the claims are amended by re-issue without unreasonable delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification discloses but the claims omit subject-matter, that omission is strong evidence of deliberate exclusion; delay in seeking re-issue after gaining knowledge of the omission supports an inference of abandonment and may bar reclamation in equity or by re-issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable delay (laches) can bar a re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay by the patentee in applying for a re-issue after discovering (or when he ought to have discovered) the defect may constitute laches and disable the patentee from obtaining or enforcing a re-issued patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine whether the patentee had knowledge or was chargeable with knowledge (imputed by reasonable inspection) and whether third parties gained intervening rights. If the defect was apparent on the face of the patent, delay is less excusable; if not discoverable despite reasonable vigilance, longer delay may be tolerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge or constructive notice imputed by reasonable inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reasonable inspection of the issued patent would have informed the patentee of the omission or narrowness of the claims, the law imputes knowledge and the patentee is chargeable from issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions (e.g., Wollensak v. Reiher; cases cited) hold that the patentee must promptly examine his patent and that failure to act after notice (actual or imputable) amounts to laches. The standard is what a person reasonably diligent in management of their own interests would discover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening rights of third parties affect the permissibility of re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: The actions and assertions of others (third parties) cannot deprive a patentee of the privilege of a re-issue unless the patentee had or should have had knowledge of the defect and delay would prejudice those intervening interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When others have invested or acted in reliance on the original claims, courts weigh the effects of delay and intervening rights; a period of inactivity that would have been acceptable absent antagonistic interests may be insufficient when others have adopted/use the unprotected subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue rights judged by facts as of the date of the original application/patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute makes the actions and attempts of the inventor at the date of the original application the sole criterion of his right to a re-issue; later acts of others do not change the basic statutory inquiry into inadvertence at the original date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While courts can consider equity, the core legal entitlement to a re-issue depends on the state of facts at the original application/patent date (e.g., whether the omission arose from inadvertence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between adding new matter and correcting a misstatement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one thing to enlarge a claim by inserting matter never before contained in it; it is quite another to amend a misstatement to reflect what the original disclosure already supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts maintain a strict distinction: correction of a misstatement supported by the original disclosure may be permitted (subject to delay rules), whereas inserting genuinely new matter is forbidden. Judicial construction determines whether a proposed amendment is corrective or adds new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: If defect is apparent on face of patent, immediate remedy required
rubrics_metrics.description: When the discrepancy between the invention and the claims is apparent upon examination of the patent, the patentee is chargeable with immediate knowledge and must pursue remedy without delay; otherwise laches will bar re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Miller v. Brass and related cases: a defect evident on first inspection leaves no excuse for delay, and courts will declare re-issues obtained after unreasonable delay void as an abuse of the re-issue power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence is required but statutes do not prescribe absolute timetables; reasonableness is fact-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither the statutes of 1832/1836/1870 nor the Revised Statutes make diligence per se an absolute condition in all circumstances; however, the courts assess the reasonableness of delay in light of the patentee's knowledge and surrounding circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long periods of delay have sometimes been excused depending on facts, but many decisions sustain refusals after long delays—courts use laches/equitable principles when statutes are silent or ambiguous about time periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot be used to claim new uses or new modes of use after unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue obtained after unreasonable delay cannot validly claim a new use or a claim whose novelty rests on a new mode of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Gardner v. Herz) hold that attempts to claim a new mode or use in a re-issue after delay are invalid. The law distinguishes between broadening to cover originally intended subject-matter and expanding to capture new uses discovered later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot change the fundamental category of invention after long delay (examples: mechanism -> process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have refused re-issues which try to convert a patent of one type (e.g., for mechanism) into a different type (e.g., a process) long after issuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Scrivner v. Oakland Gas Co. and related decisions: where the inventions are different in kind, a late re-issue to change category is impermissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity requirement: re-issue limited to what patentee attempted to describe or claim originally
rubrics_metrics.description: The re-issue may be altered or enlarged to cover the entire invention which the patentee attempted to embrace in his original patent, provided the re-issue is sought within a period consistent with the original intention to protect the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court treats as permissible only those amendments that relate to matter the patentee genuinely tried to describe/claim originally; the identity of the subject-matter between original disclosure and proposed re-issue is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial construction required where misstatement permits multiple interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is misstated in a way that allows several constructions—some of which would include the omitted matter and some which would exclude it—judicial interpretation is required to determine whether correction is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ordinary claim interpretation may be ambiguous, courts determine whether the misstatement is correctable without introducing new matter; the outcome affects whether the re-issue is an enlargement or a corrective amendment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matters described but not claimed may be dedicated to the public and strengthen public reliance over time
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patentee receives his patent and fails to claim parts of the disclosed invention, those unclaimed parts may be treated in law as dedicated to the public; every day that passes increases the strength of public reliance and the barrier to later expansion by re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issued patent is a public instrument; if the patentee holds back claiming certain disclosed elements, the public acquires the undoubted right to use them and courts are reluctant to permit later re-issues that would upset reliance and vested interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervening rights alone do not bar re-issue unless patentee had or should have had knowledge of the defect
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of third-party use or patents is not sufficient to defeat a re-issue; the patentee's knowledge or chargeability with knowledge of his patent's defect and his delay determine whether intervening rights create a bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether the patentee, when he attained knowledge, had a duty to amend without unreasonable delay to avoid impairing third-party rights; antagonistic interests make shorter delays necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific fact-pattern exceptions and time thresholds are case-dependent (examples cited)
rubrics_metrics.description: A number of cases articulate specific limits (e.g., no allowance after 8-9 years unless original claimed the matter; inability to re-issue after 14 years to claim an improvement; re-issue to cover machine part without claimed use invalid after ~3 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These temporal rules are illustrative of how courts have applied the general principles; they demonstrate that long delays (multi-year periods) often give rise to invalidation of re-issues, but exact thresholds vary by facts and case law cited (e.g., Clements v. Odorless Excavating Apparatus Co.; Sickels v. Falls Co.; Reay v. Raynor).
